passage: Siddharth, you say you can't question your director because you admire him too much. Let me tell you about Mr Lobo. I was twenty-five, a junior engineer, and he was the man I wanted to become. One day he declared that the new bridge pillars needed no extra testing; he'd built fifty bridges. I admired him, and I also had soil reports on my desk that worried me. So I asked, "Sir, how did you decide that? I'd like to learn." He explained. Then I said, "May I show you something from this week's soil tests?" He read them for a long time. We tested. He was right about two pillars and wrong about one. He shook my hand afterwards. Respect him, beta. Just don't hand him your eyes. Your Manoj uncle learned that at twenty-five.

qa.q: What was on young Manoj's desk that worried him?
qa.a: Soil reports on his desk worried him.

qa.q: What does young Manoj's 'I'd like to learn' show about how he felt toward Mr Lobo?
qa.a: He calls him the man he wanted to become and asked, 'I'd like to learn', showing respect even while doubting the claim.

qa.q: What steps from Manoj's story can Siddharth use with his director?
qa.a: Ask how the director reached the claim, then politely offer the evidence, keeping respect for the person separate from the idea.

qa.q: How did Mr Lobo respond to being questioned?
qa.a: Mr Lobo explained, read the reports for a long time, agreed to test, and shook Manoj's hand afterwards.

grounding: An uncle recalls asking, at twenty-five, how an admired senior reached a claim, offering soil data politely, and finding him partly right.

passage: Five minutes before the client walked in, Mohit, the agency's creative head, tapped the storyboard. "Our buyers are mostly retired people. Everyone knows that. Keep the ad slow and serious." Sudha had admired Mohit since her internship; his campaigns were the reason she'd joined. She also had last month's survey open on her tablet. With the clock ticking, she kept it short. "Mohit, can I ask how we got that picture of the buyers? I want to be sure I'm seeing it right." He shrugged. "Twenty years of experience." "That counts for a lot," she said. "This survey shows almost half our buyers are under thirty. Could we add one faster version, just in case?" Mohit squinted at the chart, then sighed. "Fine. Two versions. You present the second." The door opened.

qa.q: What did last month's survey show?
qa.a: Almost half our buyers are under thirty.

qa.q: How does Sudha feel about Mohit while she questions him?
qa.a: She still admires him, since his campaigns were why she joined, but trusts the survey enough to raise it. 🙂

qa.q: Which part of Sudha's approach worked best under the time pressure?
qa.a: Asking how the claim was reached, then offering one chart and a small 'just in case' option, kept it short, respectful and hard to refuse.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel after squinting at the chart?
qa.a: Mohit may feel a little caught out but also respected, since she praised his experience and only asked for a second version.

grounding: Under time pressure, a young professional politely asks how a senior reached a claim, shows data, and keeps her admiration intact.

passage: At a crowded seminar hall in Bengaluru's city planning office, Professor Varun Rao, whose textbook Pema had read three times in college, told the room that cycle lanes never work in Indian cities. "People won't use them. I've studied this for thirty years." Several heads nodded. Pema, twenty-six and eight months into her job, felt her heart speed up. She raised her hand. "Sir, your book is the reason I joined planning," she began. "Could you tell us how that conclusion was reached? I ask because our team counted riders on the new Jayanagar lane last month." She held up a printout: numbers had tripled in a year. Professor Rao studied it. "Interesting. Different from my older studies. Send me the data?" Afterwards a junior colleague whispered, "How did you dare?" Pema smiled. "I didn't argue with him. Just with the idea."

qa.q: What did Pema's team count on the Jayanagar lane?
qa.a: They counted riders on the new Jayanagar lane, and numbers had tripled in a year.

qa.q: What does Pema's speeding heart suggest as she raises her hand?
qa.a: It suggests she felt nervous challenging someone she admired, yet trusted her data enough to speak.

qa.q: How did Pema keep her challenge respectful?
qa.a: She thanked him for his book, asked how he reached the conclusion, and offered her count instead of saying he was wrong.

qa.q: How does the junior colleague see Pema's question?
qa.a: The junior colleague sees it as daring, as if questioning a senior were risky, while Pema sees it as arguing only with the idea.

grounding: A young planner asks a famous professor how he reached a claim and offers new data, respecting him while questioning the idea.

passage:
"Mausi, can I ask something about what you said at dinner?"
Ishita Mausi, principal of a school for twenty years, put down her teacup. "Ask, Aditi."
"You said board toppers always come from the science stream. How did you reach that?"
"Thirty years in schools, beta. I've seen it."
"You've seen far more than me," Aditi said. "I just happened to look at our district's results for work last month. Can I show you?" She turned her laptop around. "Top ten this year: four science, three commerce, three humanities."
Mausi leaned in, frowning. "Hm. In my school, the science children did better."
"That might be true for your school. I'd love to know why. Better teachers, maybe?"
Mausi laughed. "You're arguing with me in my own house."
"I'm not arguing with you," Aditi said, smiling. "Just with that sentence. You're still the smartest person at this table."

qa.q: How many of the district's top ten were from the science stream this year?
qa.a: Four science, three commerce, three humanities, so four were from science.

qa.q: What does Aditi's way of speaking suggest she felt about Mausi, even while disagreeing?
qa.a: It suggests real respect and affection: she asked permission first, said Mausi had seen far more than her, and ended by calling Mausi the smartest person at the table while disagreeing only with the sentence.

qa.q: What steps did Aditi take that made the challenge work?
qa.a: She asked how Mausi reached the claim, offered district results as evidence politely, and stayed curious about why Mausi's school might be different.

qa.q: How might Ishita Mausi feel after the conversation?
qa.a: Mausi seems a little surprised but amused, laughing rather than offended, since Aditi separated respect for her from disagreeing with her claim.

grounding: It shows a professional asking how an elder reached a claim, offering evidence politely, and keeping respect for the person separate from the idea.

passage:
I'm Zubin, a junior structural engineer, and I have admired Afreen ma'am since my first day at the firm. She's designed half the bridges in our district. So when she said at the review, "The old soil report from 2015 is enough; we don't need a new test," my first instinct was to nod.
But I'd walked that site the week before. The riverbank had shifted after two heavy monsoons.
After the meeting, I knocked on her cabin. "Ma'am, can I ask how we decided the 2015 report still fits?"
She looked up, a little surprised. "The soil there hasn't changed in decades."
"You know that ground better than I do," I said. "But I took photos last week. The bank has moved." I put them on her desk.
She studied them for a long time. Then she picked up the phone and asked for a new test. As I left she said, "Good. Keep doing that, young man."

qa.q: What had happened to the riverbank after two heavy monsoons?
qa.a: The riverbank had shifted after two heavy monsoons.

qa.q: What was Zubin's first instinct at the review, and why?
qa.a: Zubin's first instinct was to nod, because he admired Afreen ma'am and she had designed half the bridges in the district.

qa.q: How did Zubin raise the concern in a way that kept both respect and accuracy?
qa.a: He asked privately how the decision was reached, acknowledged that she knew the ground better, and then showed his photos as evidence.

qa.q: How might Afreen ma'am feel about Zubin after he left?
qa.a: Afreen ma'am seems to appreciate him more, since she ordered the new test and told him to keep doing that.

grounding: A junior engineer describes asking a respected senior how a claim was reached, offering evidence politely, and separating respect from agreement.
